title: Case study: Niger, a high dependent population

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: One required case study: Niger, a country with a high dependent population, the structure, its cause and its implications.

blocks.heading: The structure and its cause
blocks.text: Niger, in the Sahel south of the Sahara, has one of the world's highest dependent populations: nearly half its people are under 15, around 44 per cent in the early 2020s, against a small economically active share, so the dependency ratio is high and each worker supports many children. The cause is the birth rate, around 45 per 1000, which keeps adding large cohorts of children while the adult group stays thin, because fertility has not yet fallen: girls marry young, average only a few years of school, and children support their parents on the family farms. The pyramid this builds has a very wide base and a very narrow top, but the marks are in the groups and shares, not the silhouette.

blocks.heading: The implications
blocks.text: The implications of Niger's structure follow from the ratio. A school-age cohort too large for the classrooms and teachers available means children are taught in shifts and classes of dozens, so learning thins out. Clinics are stretched by child and maternal care, because the patients are mostly young, and too few adults exist to fund it all: the tax-paying, farming, working group is the thin band in the middle of the pyramid. So the country faces a double task, educating and caring for the widest generation it has ever had with the narrowest workforce it has ever had.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: This case study answers any 7-mark question that names a country with a high dependent population, and Niger is also the high natural growth case in topic 1.1: the same birth rate that grows the population builds the young structure here. A contrasting ageing case is Japan, in topic 1.1's case studies.
